title: Virtuele Brigade
challenge: I joined a VR training sim that had been in the works for years, and my job was to bolt multiplayer and VR support onto it, quite a task.
built: A lot of careful surgery later, instructors could run shared scenarios together and even create their own. It gets wheeled out at events and will replace the previous software package used in training new KMar agents, which I’m pretty proud of.
outcome: Multiplayer VR, retrofitted into a living system
lesson: Adding tech to a system that already exists is often harder than starting from scratch. Before i implement a feature i should ask: 'will this even be maintained?'

title: Alliander HoloLens suite
challenge: Alliander has to drop two-tonne transformers into neighbourhoods where people are not waiting for an ugly box in view. Paper plans were used to decide on a location, this can be improved upon.
built: We duct-taped RTK GPS, an Android phone, a HoloLens and a backend together so specialists could literally see the transformer floating in exactly the right spot on the real street, to the centimetre. The sighting can be saved and reviewed, visuals give an immediate idea of the resulting environment.
outcome: Holograms that line up with the world to the cm
lesson: The tech was the easy half. Getting it to fit how an organisation actually works, day to day, was the real puzzle and eventual downfall of this project, it did not catch on due to impracticallities. If it were up to me i would not choose a Hololens but an iPad instead.

title: Alliander digital twin
challenge: Engineers were driving out to the same sites over and over, to check the measurements and sizing of a transformerhouse
built: I built a web tool that mashes laser scans, 360° photos and equipment models together, so they could walk the site from their desk and try things out before anyone got in a van.
outcome: Site visits you can do from your chair
lesson: Technically it worked great, but the organisation wasn’t quite ready to change how it worked so it never fully landed.

title: ARCam
challenge: Niantic wanted to hand event visitors a real photo with their favourite characters — Pokémon, Monster Hunter beasts, basketball stars, the Niantic mascot — and it had to work first time, on a busy show floor, in a different city every other week.
built: ARCam — an AR photo installation I built at Wonderment for Niantic. An iPad running the Lightship SDK drops the characters into the scene through a viewfinder that came in a few builds, from a sturdy pedestal to a portable tripod rig. Two modes: take a photo with the characters — the main event — or pan around to spot location-based highlights out in the world.
outcome: 16 cities worldwide, packed in a suitcase
lesson: Location-based AR is a systems-integration problem dressed up as a graphics demo: the physical world is your least reliable dependency, so you end up owning everything — tracking, databases, web, audio, performance, devices, UX, 3D, even the electronics and the screws. The backend was a punt I built on a hunch — vibe-coded years before that was a phrase; it fell over on day one and then ran flawlessly, which taught me how much value you can add just by taking the initiative early. And living out of a suitcase across sixteen cities taught me what ‘delivering’ really means: a thing that survives heat, bad Wi-Fi and a knocked tripod, not just a thing that works on your desk.

fieldNotes.label: Internet
fieldNotes.body: Wi-Fi congestion and blocked traffic at venues — it needs an offline mode.

fieldNotes.label: Heat
fieldNotes.body: iPads overheating (Cannes) and batteries draining fast (Berlin).

fieldNotes.label: Social
fieldNotes.body: Cultural differences in how people queue and pose for the camera.

fieldNotes.label: Physical
fieldNotes.body: Knocked tripods, yanked cables, dropped iPads — and screws that didn’t hold, bought fresh in the city.

title: Wonderment location XR
challenge: We kept circling the same question: what can you actually build when digital content is pinned to a real place — and what quietly falls apart the moment you step outside the lab?
built: A run of location-based experiments — GPS- and map-anchored AR prototypes that tie content to real coordinates, poking at how it behaves out in the wild rather than on a tidy desk.
outcome: A stack of location-anchored AR prototypes
lesson: The real world is a messy test lab — GPS drifts, places change, people wander into frame. Designing for that mess up front beats pretending it isn't there.

title: DTT Amsterdam
challenge: A studio shipping client work in every format under the sun — one week an educational book that plays, the next a VR piece or an AR demo — all of it needing to actually work, not just look good in a pitch.
built: I worked across a run of projects here: an interactive edu play book, an OSR VR experience, and an AR sample & showcase app that shows off what the tech can do.
outcome: A shelf of shipped AR / VR / app projects
lesson: Bouncing between wildly different projects teaches you to spot the shared bones underneath — the patterns that carry from a playful book straight over to a VR sim.

title: Lightship Drive
challenge: Show off shared, multiplayer AR on a noisy trade-show floor, about the most difficult environment you can imagine for tracking.
built: A multiplayer AR racing game with spectator screens, synced audio and a server holding it all together. People racing little AR cars across a real table together.
outcome: AR races on a show floor (and they actually worked)
lesson: Build assuming things will fail, because on a show floor they absolutely will. In this case the server SDK was brand new and cut off sessions after some 10 minutes, not seeing a fix i introduced a 'you won! give the phone to the next visitor' popup when the server decided to close.

title: Zwijsen AR books
challenge: Kids’ books that come alive when you point a phone at them — and, crucially, survive being used by actual kids.
built: I designed, built and shipped the AR and audiobook apps tied to printed books via QR codes — the whole thing, idea to app store, on both iOS and Android.
outcome: Ended up on tens of thousands of phones
lesson: Owning something end to end teaches you the whole lifecycle — and that the last 10% (support, store reviews, that one cursed device) is somehow most of the work.

title: Popcore games
challenge: Hyper-casual games live and die on speed — ship fast, test, kill it if it flops, repeat.
built: I built gameplay, multiplayer and little tools for the designers inside an ECS setup, on games like Parking Jam and Pull the Pin.
lesson: Sometimes shipping fast and iterating beats elegant code by a mile. The market really doesn’t care how pretty your architecture is.

title: Philips medical XR & AI
challenge: Could emerging XR and AI actually be useful in a clinical setting — or were we just making cool demos and calling it research?
built: I poked at a few answers: VR equipment demos, some Vision Pro experiments, and a synthetic-data project that generated fake humans in Unreal to train heartbeat-detection from plain video.
lesson: Research is as much about finding out what you shouldn’t build as what you should. “This isn’t worth it” is a real, useful result — even if it feels anticlimactic.

title: Amsterdam AI guides
challenge: I wanted to know if an AI tour guide could feel like a person instead of a chatbot — fictional Amsterdam locals you could actually talk to.
built: A prototype stitching together speech-to-text, an LLM, text-to-speech and facial animation into characters you hold an honest conversation with, in AR.
outcome: AI locals you can actually chat with
lesson: Just because you can automate the human out of something doesn’t mean you should. Technically working and emotionally working are very different bars.

title: Custom AR framework
challenge: Back before AR Foundation existed, ARKit and ARCore were two separate worlds, and cross-platform AR meant maintaining two codebases. Annoying.
built: For my graduation I built a framework that unified both behind one API and poked at cloud anchors and sharing AR between phones.
outcome: Two AR platforms, one tidy API
lesson: Building the tool underneath often creates more value than solving the one problem in front of you. I’ve been reaching for that lesson ever since.
